834.title: Fra Angelico (d. 1455)
834.hook: a Dominican friar who painted the Annunciation on his brothers' cell walls
834.howItsDone: Catholics pray with images in churches and homes, and the Angelus, prayed by some at morning, noon and evening, recalls the Annunciation with the angel's greeting and Mary's answer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the printing press, and the great book it's remembered for. Your line was the first book printed. What page did you read slowly? Day eight hundred thirty-four.

Before dawn, in a convent in Florence, a friar wakes in a small bare cell: a bed, a window, a desk. Before he sees anything else, he sees a scene from the Gospel on his wall. Not hung there. Painted right into the plaster. Down the corridor, cell after cell has its own. The painter was a friar of that same house, a brother who walked the same corridor. People called him Fra Angelico. Today's name is his.
screen: `A FRIAR WAKES BEFORE DAWN.` → `A PAINTING IN THE PLASTER.` → `THE GOSPEL, FIRST THING.`

segments.voice: Start with who he was. Fra Angelico was a Dominican friar, a brother of the Order of Preachers, and a painter. Fra means brother. Angelico, angelic, is the name people gave him, for his work and for his life. Next, the walls. At the convent of San Marco in Florence, he painted scenes from the life of Christ in his brothers' cells. They were not there for visitors. They were for the friar who lived with them, to pray with. Few figures, plain backgrounds, a great deal of quiet. Then, the Annunciation. At the top of the stairs to the cells, he painted the moment in Luke's Gospel when the angel Gabriel comes to Mary. In the Douay-Rheims, the angel says, "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee." And Mary answers, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." In the painting, the angel leans in, Mary leans toward him with her arms folded across her chest, and nothing else in the scene moves. Some viewers read it as the moment before her yes. Finally, why it counts as prayer. Giorgio Vasari, who wrote lives of the Italian artists after him, says Fra Angelico prayed before he took up his brush. The Church later beatified him and named him a patron of artists. A Dominican's work is to preach. He preached without a sermon, on a wall, to one brother at a time.
screen: `A DOMINICAN FRIAR AND PAINTER.` · `THE GOSPEL ON THE CELL WALLS.` · `HAIL, FULL OF GRACE.` · `HE PRAYED BEFORE HE PAINTED.` · then, large: `PRAYER IN PAINT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at one Annunciation. Before the sit, find one: Fra Angelico's from San Marco if you can, or any other, on a screen, a card, a church window, or in memory. Look for a minute without analyzing. Where does the light fall? Which way is each one leaning? Then close your eyes and keep the picture. If you pray, you can pray the angel's greeting, hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee. If you don't, just rest in the quiet of the picture. The bell holds the time.
Fra Angelico. A Dominican friar in Florence who painted the Gospel on his brothers' cell walls, so they could pray with it. Today's word.
Your line: prayer in paint. Tonight, put one image where you'll see it first thing tomorrow morning, the way the friars woke up to theirs. Day eight hundred thirty-four.

835.title: The Renaissance popes, honestly
835.hook: some popes of this age were worldly, scheming and corrupt
835.howItsDone: At Mass, Catholics pray for the pope and their bishop by name, and the Mass often begins with a confession of sin said together; the Church also holds penitential liturgies asking forgiveness for the sins of its members.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fra Angelico, who painted the Gospel on his brothers' cell walls. Your line was prayer in paint. What image did you wake up to this morning? Day eight hundred thirty-five.

A cardinal's red hat, given to a pope's young relative. A pope who rides out in armor at the head of his own troops. A pope whose children are known by name in Rome, and who works to set them up with lands and titles. These aren't rumors invented by the Church's enemies. They are part of the record of the Renaissance papacy, and Catholic historians tell them too. Today's word is the habit that ran through several of those stories: nepotism.
screen: `A RED HAT FOR A RELATIVE.` → `A POPE IN ARMOR.` → `A POPE'S CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Nepotism means handing out offices, money and power to your relatives because they're family, not because they're fit. In this age, some popes made nephews cardinals, built fortunes for their families, and ran the Papal States like a family business. Next, the names. Sixtus the Fourth raised nephews to cardinal. Alexander the Sixth, born Rodrigo Borgia, had children and worked hard to advance them. Julius the Second led troops in person. Leo the Tenth spent lavishly. They were not all alike, and some also paid for art and learning that people still travel to see. But the corruption was real, and it helped set the stage for storms that were coming. Then, what the Church says about itself. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church is holy, and at the same time always in need of being purified, because it holds sinners in its embrace. Catholic teaching places the Church's holiness in Christ, not in the virtue of its leaders. Pope John Paul the Second later asked forgiveness, publicly, for sins committed by the Church's members through history. Finally, the Scriptures. The first letter of John says, in the Douay-Rheims, "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." And Peter, the rock Catholics see the Church built on, denied Jesus on the night of his arrest. Luke tells it without softening: "Peter going out, wept bitterly." The Gospels did not leave his failure out of the story. They kept his tears in it too.
screen: `NEPOTISM: OFFICES FOR FAMILY.` · `SIXTUS, ALEXANDER, JULIUS, LEO.` · `HOLY, AND ALWAYS BEING PURIFIED.` · `PETER WEPT BITTERLY.` · then, large: `THE CHURCH HAS SINNED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for leaders who fail. Before the sit, bring to mind one leader who has let people down: in a church, a government, a company, a family. Maybe it's you. Don't excuse it, and don't spit on it. Take one slow breath. Hold two things at once: the harm that was done, and the person who did it. If you pray, you can pray for them and for the people they hurt, or simply say, Lord, have mercy, with them in mind. If you don't, just hold both, honestly, without looking away. The bell holds the time.
Nepotism. Handing out offices and power to relatives because they're family; a failing of some Renaissance popes. Today's word.
Your line: the church has sinned. Today, when a failure comes up, yours or anyone's, name it plainly instead of defending it or sneering at it. Day eight hundred thirty-five.

836.title: The Sistine ceiling (1508–1512)
836.hook: Michelangelo paints creation, the hand of God reaching to Adam's
836.howItsDone: The Sistine Chapel is still used for papal liturgies, and the cardinals meet there in conclave to elect a new pope; pilgrims and visitors are asked to keep silence beneath the ceiling.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Renaissance popes, told honestly. Your line was the church has sinned. What failure did you name plainly, without defending it or sneering? Day eight hundred thirty-six.

High above the floor of a chapel in the Vatican, a man stands on a scaffold with his head bent back and his arm raised, paint dripping onto his face. He thinks of himself as a sculptor. In a comic poem about the job, he complains of his aching neck and his beard pointing up at heaven, and insists he is no painter. The pope who hired him was Julius the Second, yesterday's pope in armor. The painter was Michelangelo, and what he left overhead is today's word: the Sistine ceiling.
screen: `A MAN ON A SCAFFOLD, HEAD BENT BACK.` → `I AM NO PAINTER.` → `HIRED BY JULIUS THE SECOND.`

segments.voice: Start with the ceiling. Michelangelo filled it with the opening chapters of Genesis: God dividing light from darkness, the sun and moon, Adam, Eve, the fall, Noah. Prophets and sibyls sit around the edges, as if waiting. Next, the famous panel. Genesis says, in the Douay-Rheims, "God created man to his own image." And in its second telling: "the Lord God formed man of the slime of the earth: and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." Michelangelo doesn't paint breath. He paints hands. Then, the gap. Adam lies on bare ground, his arm lifted, his hand loose at the wrist. God rushes toward him through the air, arm stretched out, finger extended. And the two fingers do not touch. There is a sliver of empty ceiling between them. Michelangelo never explained it. Some readers see the instant before life passes across. Others notice the contrast: God straining forward, Adam barely lifting a finger. Others see the whole human story in that gap, made for God and not quite reaching. Finally, why it still matters. The Sistine Chapel is still a working chapel, and the cardinals gather under this ceiling to elect a pope. Yesterday's honest list included Julius. Today's includes what he paid for. The Church holds both, and the ceiling holds both hands, almost touching.
screen: `GENESIS ON THE CEILING.` · `FORMED, AND GIVEN THE BREATH OF LIFE.` · `TWO HANDS, AND A GAP.` · `STILL A WORKING CHAPEL.` · then, large: `ALMOST TOUCHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the two hands. Before the sit, find the Creation of Adam on a screen, or call it up from memory, or simply hold your own two hands out in front of you, fingertips almost meeting. Look at the gap, and let your breath slow. Ask which hand is closer to your day today: the one reaching hard, or the one barely lifting. Either is worth noticing. If you pray, you can let the words from Genesis, the breath of life, ride on your breathing. If you don't, just rest in the space between. The bell holds the time.
The Sistine ceiling. Michelangelo's painted Genesis above the pope's chapel, where God's hand reaches for Adam's and doesn't quite touch. Today's word.
Your line: almost touching. Today, notice one relationship that's close but not quite there, and close the gap by one small reach: a call, a hand on a shoulder, a word. Day eight hundred thirty-six.

837.hook: Spain expels its Jews, and ships reach the Americas; both shaped centuries of suffering
837.howItsDone: Catholic memory of these wrongs is public as well as personal: John Paul II's Day of Pardon in the Jubilee year 2000 confessed sins against the people of Israel and against the rights of peoples, and Pope Francis has asked forgiveness for crimes against the native peoples of the Americas during the conquest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sistine ceiling: a painted finger, and the hand of God reaching for it. Your line was almost touching. What was almost within reach yesterday? Day eight hundred thirty-seven.

Two documents from one year. The first is a royal decree, signed by Ferdinand and Isabella, the king and queen of Spain. It orders every Jew in their kingdoms to leave by a fixed deadline and never return. Only baptism would let a family stay. The second is the opening of a sailor's journal. Christopher Columbus writes to those same two monarchs, and in a single stretch of thought he mentions the Jews being driven out, and his own orders to sail west. Same rulers. Same year. Same page. Today's word is that year.
screen: `A DECREE: LEAVE, AND NEVER RETURN.` → `A SAILOR'S JOURNAL.` → `SAME RULERS, SAME PAGE.`

segments.voice: Start with the decree. Jewish families had lived in Spain for generations: doctors, weavers, translators, neighbors. Now they had until the deadline to choose. Some were baptized and stayed, and they and their children often lived afterward under suspicion from the Inquisition. Others sold what they could, left homes and graves behind, and went out to Portugal, North Africa, the lands of the Ottoman sultan. Their descendants, called Sephardic Jews, carried the language and songs of Spain with them. Next, the journal. Columbus reaches an island in the Caribbean, and the people there, the Taíno, come out to meet the ships. He writes that they are gentle, that they carry no weapons, and almost in the same breath that they would make good servants. That sentence turned out to be a forecast. What followed for the peoples of the islands and the mainland was forced labor, war and disease, and whole communities were lost. Then, the hard part for Catholics. Both stories were told by their tellers in the language of faith. The decree spoke of protecting the faith; the voyage spoke of carrying it. Catholic teaching today says plainly that faith must never be forced, and recent popes have asked forgiveness for wrongs done by the Church's members. Finally, the word for today. Remembering honestly is not the same as hating the past. It means letting both documents stand, without cutting either. Psalm one hundred twenty-nine begins, "Out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord: Lord, hear my voice." It is a prayer that fits exiles. It fits people whose land was taken, too. Honest memory makes room for both voices.
screen: `A DECREE, AND FAMILIES ON THE ROAD.` · `GENTLE PEOPLE, AND A FORECAST.` · `BOTH TOLD IN THE LANGUAGE OF FAITH.` · `LETTING BOTH DOCUMENTS STAND.` · then, large: `OUT OF THE DEPTHS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the descendants of both. Settle, and breathe slowly. First, bring to mind the Jewish families who walked out of Spain, and the families today who come from them. Stay there a few breaths. Then bring to mind the Taíno and the peoples of the Americas, and those living today who come from them. If you pray, you can pray for both, using the psalm's words, out of the depths. If you don't, simply hold the two groups of people in your attention, one after the other, without hurrying. The bell holds the time.
Fourteen ninety-two. The year Spain's Jews were told to be baptized or leave, and the year ships from Spain reached the Americas. Today's word.
Your line: remember honestly. Today, when a story gets told about the past, at work or at home, ask once: who else was there, and how would they tell it? Day eight hundred thirty-seven.

838.title: Bartolomé de las Casas (1484–1566)
838.hook: a colonist and slaveholder who converted and spent fifty years defending Indigenous peoples
838.howItsDone: Las Casas is not a canonized saint; Catholics remember him as a Dominican friar and bishop who defended Indigenous peoples, and a cause for his beatification has been opened.

segments.voice: Yesterday, 1492: a decree that sent Spain's Jews into exile, and a journal that called the Taíno good servants. Your line was remember honestly. Whose side of a story did you ask about? Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

A priest on the island of Cuba sits down to write a sermon for Pentecost. He owns land, and Indigenous people work it for him under a colonial grant called an encomienda. He is, by his own later account, as busy with his mines and fields as anyone. He opens the book of Ecclesiasticus for his text, and a few lines stop him cold. Years later he would write the whole scene down himself. Today's word is his name: Bartolomé de las Casas.
screen: `A SERMON FOR PENTECOST.` → `A PRIEST WITH LAND AND LABORERS.` → `A FEW LINES STOP HIM.`

segments.voice: First, the lines. In the Douay-Rheims, Ecclesiasticus says: "The bread of the needy is the life of the poor: he that defraudeth them thereof is a man of blood." Las Casas read that and saw his own fields. The people working them were the needy, and their bread was going to him. Second, what he had already heard. In his History of the Indies he admits that a Dominican friar had once refused him absolution because he held Indigenous people in his service, and that he had argued back. The words had not landed then. Now they did. Third, what he did. He gave up the people granted to him and went to the governor to say so. Then he preached it from the pulpit, telling his neighbors that holding the islanders this way put their souls in danger. The neighbors, he says, were astonished, and some thought him foolish. He went on to cross the ocean to argue before the court of Spain, later joined the Dominicans himself, and wrote a short and furious account of the destruction of the Indies. Fourth, and this is the part that makes him trustworthy: he changed more than once. At one stage he had suggested that enslaved Africans be brought to do the work, to spare the Indigenous people. Later, in his History, he wrote that he regretted it, because the same injustice was being done to them. A man who could admit that about himself was still changing. The words in Ecclesiasticus had not changed. What changed was the reader.
screen: `THE BREAD OF THE NEEDY.` · `A FRIAR HAD ALREADY WARNED HIM.` · `HE GAVE THEM UP, AND SAID SO.` · `HE CHANGED AGAIN, AND ADMITTED IT.` · then, large: `A MAN OF BLOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one place your mind could change for justice. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you've always done, bought, said or believed without looking at who pays for it. It doesn't need to be large. Just look at it honestly, the way Las Casas looked at his fields. Ask who the needy are in that picture. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to change. If you don't, simply let yourself consider it for the length of the bell. The bell holds the time.
Bartolomé de las Casas. A priest who held Indigenous laborers, read a line about the bread of the needy, gave them up, and spent the rest of his life defending their peoples. Today's word.

839.title: Sublimis Deus (1537)
839.hook: Pope Paul III declares Indigenous peoples free and rational, often ignored by colonists
839.howItsDone: Catholics point to Sublimis Deus in Church teaching on human dignity; Indigenous Catholics and their bishops have cited it, alongside later papal apologies, when speaking about the history of the Americas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bartolomé de las Casas, the priest who read a line about the bread of the needy and gave up his laborers. Your line was he changed. Did you say out loud where you'd been wrong? Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

Some questions should never need asking. On the island of Hispaniola, a Dominican friar named Antonio de Montesinos climbed into the pulpit on a Sunday in Advent and put one to the Spanish settlers in front of him. Are these not men? Do they not have rational souls? Las Casas later wrote down the sermon and how angry the congregation was. Years afterward, the question reached Rome, and a pope answered it in writing. Today's word is the first two words of his answer: Sublimis Deus.
screen: `A FRIAR IN THE PULPIT.` → `ARE THESE NOT MEN?` → `ROME ANSWERS IN WRITING.`

segments.voice: Begin with the title. The letter is named by its first words, and they mean the sublime God, the God on high. The letter opens not with the Americas but with God, who made people able to know him. Next, the lie it names. Paul III writes that some, moved by the enemy of the human race, have claimed that the peoples of the West and South should be treated like dumb animals, as if unable to receive the faith, and used that claim to put them to work. The letter calls this out for what it is. Then, the answer itself. The pope declares that these peoples are truly human, able to understand and receive the faith, and that they may not be deprived of their liberty or of their property, even if they are outside the faith. And the faith is to be offered to them by preaching and by the example of a good life, not by force. Underneath it is a line the letter itself leans on: Jesus sending out his apostles. In the Douay-Rheims: "Going therefore, teach ye all nations." All, the pope writes, without exception, because all are able to receive the faith. Last, the gap. A letter from Rome is ink. In the colonies, men with land and gold had every reason to look away, and the bull's promises were resisted and, on the ground, often not kept. Las Casas and others kept pressing its point before royal councils. So Sublimis Deus is two things at once: a clear statement of what the Church said about human dignity, and a reminder that saying it is never the end of the work.
screen: `THE GOD ON HIGH.` · `A LIE CALLED BY ITS NAME.` · `FREE, AND OWNERS OF WHAT THEY HAVE.` · `INK, AND THE GAP AFTER IT.` · then, large: `TEACH YE ALL NATIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold Indigenous peoples in mind. Sit comfortably and breathe. Bring to mind the Indigenous peoples of the land where you are right now, by name if you know it, or simply as the people who were here first. Think of them now, not only long ago: families, languages, elders, children. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own words, or rest with the line the pope leaned on, all nations, without exception. If you don't, let them stay in your attention, as real and present as your own neighbors. The bell holds the time.
Sublimis Deus. The sublime God. A papal letter of Paul the Third declaring that the peoples of the Americas are truly human, free, and not to be enslaved. Today's word.

840.title: Juan Diego, saint (2002)
840.hook: the Indigenous visionary of Guadalupe canonized almost five centuries later
840.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Juan Diego's feast in December, just before the feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe; pilgrims come to the basilica in Mexico City to see the tilma, and parishes across the Americas celebrate Guadalupe with Masses, processions and roses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sublimis Deus, a pope's letter answering a friar's question. Your line was they are truly human. Whose face did you give back? Today ends the week. Day eight hundred forty.

Early one morning, a man named Juan Diego is walking past a hill called Tepeyac, on his way to Mass. He hears singing, like birds, coming from the top. Then a woman's voice calls him by name, tenderly, in his own language, Nahuatl. He climbs, and finds a lady standing there, her clothes shining like the sun. The account of what follows is called the Nican Mopohua, from its opening words in Nahuatl. Today's word is the man she called: Juan Diego.
screen: `SINGING ON THE HILL.` → `CALLED BY NAME, IN NAHUATL.` → `THE NICAN MOPOHUA.`

segments.voice: First, the request. In the account, the lady says she is the Virgin Mary, and asks for a church to be built on that spot, where she can show her love to all who come. She sends Juan Diego to the bishop in the city to ask for it. Second, the refusal, and what Juan Diego says about himself. The bishop listens politely and sends him away. Juan Diego goes back up the hill and begs her to send someone important instead. In the account he calls himself a little man, a nobody, a tail, a leaf, someone others carry. Send a person of standing, he says; they will be believed. She answers that she has plenty of messengers, and she chooses him. Third, the sign. The bishop asks for proof. On the hilltop, in the cold season, Juan Diego finds flowers blooming, gathers them into his tilma, the rough cloak he wears, and carries them to the bishop. When he opens the cloak, the flowers fall out, and on the cloth is an image of the lady. That cloak hangs in the basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City. Fourth, the name. Again and again in the account, Mary calls him by tender words for the smallest, youngest child in a family. There's a line in Matthew's Gospel that fits him. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus thanks his Father, "because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones." Pope John Paul the Second declared Juan Diego a saint in Mexico City, at that same basilica. The man who asked to be replaced by someone important became the one remembered.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor an Indigenous saint. Sit and breathe, and picture Juan Diego on the road with his cloak bundled in his arms, walking toward a bishop who doubted him. Stay with him for a while. If you pray, you can ask for his prayers, or for the prayers of another Indigenous saint you know, such as Kateri Tekakwitha. If you don't, simply honor him in the quiet: a man who thought he was too small, and went anyway. The bell holds the time.
Juan Diego. The Indigenous man who, in the account of Guadalupe, carried flowers in his cloak to a doubting bishop, and was named a saint at the basilica beside that hill. Today's word.

Your line: the little one. This week went from prayer in paint, to a church that has sinned, to two hands almost touching, to remembering honestly, to a man who changed, to people who are truly human, and now to the little one. Today, do one thing you feel too small for. Day eight hundred forty.
